title: Structure à l'infini des Mg,ν [pages 1 à 90, dont table des matières] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (section 6, 'Morphismes de généralisation de graphes'). An ordinary graph is G = (S, Ã, σ, o). Here S is the set of vertices, Ã the set of oriented arcs (half-edges), σ the fixed-point-free involution reversing orientation, and o: Ã → S the origin map. The previous page attaches to G its fundamental groupoid Π1(G). Its objects are S, and its arrows s → s' are the reduced ('simple') edge-paths, i.e. homotopy classes of paths in the topological realization. Π1 is strictly functorial in G.

This page.
1. A graph morphism f: G' → G is recovered from Π1(f): Π1(G') → Π1(G), formula (42). The action of f on vertices is the action of Π1(f) on objects. The action on arcs is read off the commutative square (43): Ã(G') → Ã(G) over Fl(Π1(G')) → Fl(Π1(G)). The vertical maps are the inclusions of arcs as length-one paths, which are injective. Fl means the set of arrows.
2. Hence graph morphisms G' → G are exactly the groupoid morphisms Π1(G') → Π1(G) that send arcs of G' to arcs of G. Π1(G') is the free groupoid on the graph G'. So any assignment of arcs to arrows that respects sources and the involution extends uniquely to a groupoid morphism, and the identification is just this universal property.
3. Generalization. A 'morphisme généralisé', or 'morphisme de généralisation', of G' into G is defined (completed on the next page) as a groupoid morphism Π1(G') → Π1(G) sending each arc either to an arc or to an identity arrow. Equivalently, it sends 'elementary arrows' (identities and arcs, a set stable under inversion) to elementary arrows. This makes stability under composition evident.

Modern content. These are graph maps allowing edge contraction: a combination of folding/immersion maps and contractions of edges, loops included. This is the kind of morphism that indexes the boundary stratification of the Deligne–Mumford–Knudsen compactification of M_{g,ν}. Contracting edges of a dual graph corresponds to passing to a more general stratum (fewer nodes). That explains the name 'généralisation'. On the next page he renames it 'spécialisation', presumably thinking of the opposite direction of the specialization relation between strata.

Purpose. To set up the category of (stable) dual graphs and their contraction/specialization maps. This category governs the 'structure à l'infini', i.e. the combinatorics of boundary strata and their incidences in M̄_{g,ν}. It is presumably used to organize the fundamental groupoids at infinity (tangential base points along the boundary).
errors: The sentence 'les morphismes de G dans G'' should read 'de G' dans G', since the groupoid maps go Π1(G') → Π1(G). This is a direction slip.
Minor gap: a morphism of groupoids sending arcs to arcs must also be compatible with the involution σ. This is automatic, since the inverse of an arc is σ of it, but it is not stated.
Terminological instability: 'morphisme de généralisation' here versus 'morphisme de spécialisation' on the next page. This is a direction-convention hesitation, not a mathematical error.

Not stated here: graphs with genus decorations or legs (needed for M̄_{g,ν}) would require extra conditions under contraction (for example, genus increases when a loop is contracted). Perhaps this is handled later.

ideas.what: Graph morphisms are identified with morphisms of fundamental (free) groupoids that send arcs to arcs.
ideas.modern_name: Universal property of the free groupoid on a graph; Serre-style graphs with involution
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Higgins 1971, Serre 'Arbres, amalgames, SL2' 1977 for the graph formalism)
ideas.where_published: Not as such; graph/groupoid language appears around Esquisse d'un programme (dessins d'enfants, Teichmüller tower)

ideas.what: Generalized (contraction) morphisms of graphs, defined as groupoid morphisms sending elementary arrows (arcs or identities) to elementary arrows; closed under composition.
ideas.modern_name: Graph morphisms with edge contractions; the category of stable graphs indexing the boundary strata of M̄_{g,n}
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Deligne–Mumford/Knudsen stratification; formalized by Getzler–Kapranov (modular operads, 1998), Manin, Borisov–Manin (2007), and later Hackney–Robertson–Yau and Kock (graphical categories)
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme discusses the stratification at infinity of M_{g,ν} but, to my knowledge, not this groupoid-theoretic definition

missed.claim: A slick groupoid-theoretic definition of contraction morphisms of graphs. Groupoid maps Π1(G') → Π1(G) preserving 'elementary arrows' (arcs or identities) give the category of graphs with contractions, with composition stability immediate. The formulation is elegant, but the resulting category is standard in the modular-operad / stable-graph literature.
missed.quote: on généralise la notion de morphisme de graphes en celle de morphisme généralisé de G' dans G, (ou "morphisme de généralisation" de G' dans G)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a minor historical point. The groupoid encoding may be convenient for functorially linking dual graphs with fundamental groupoids at infinity of M̄_{g,ν}. It is not a new result.

deep.surprise_reason: Routine foundational material: free groupoid on a graph and the standard notion of edge-contraction morphisms. The only mild interest is the groupoid-based definition and Grothendieck's early use of graph categories for the boundary of M_{g,ν}.
